passage: I'm Rafiq, Reena's neighbour. I'd gone over to borrow her physics notes. Reena, sixteen, had her board exam in two days. Then the bell rang: four relatives, unannounced. Within a minute her mother called, 'Reena, chai banao, and bring the biscuits.' Reena closed her book slowly. Her brother Kunal, a year younger, stayed on the sofa with his game. Nobody called him. I watched Reena carry the tray three times, smile at every aunty and answer questions about her marks. When she came back to her desk, her pen hovered over the same line for ten minutes. Later I heard her ask her mother quietly, 'Can Kunal do the next round?' I don't know what her mother said.

qa.q: When was Reena's board exam?
qa.a: In two days.

qa.q: What does Reena's pen hovering over the same line suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt frustrated and unsettled, unable to focus after being pulled from study while her brother was left alone.

qa.q: What would be a fairer way to handle the surprise guests?
qa.a: Share the serving between Reena and Kunal, or let Kunal take this round since Reena had an exam, while still welcoming the guests warmly.

qa.q: How might Kunal see the evening, and what would change if he were called too?
qa.a: Kunal may not notice the unfairness since nobody asked him; if he were called, he would learn hosting is everyone's job and Reena would get time to study.

grounding: Shows a teenage daughter pulled from exam study to serve tea to unexpected relatives while her brother is left alone, raising the question of fairness in who serves guests.

passage:
Tuesday: Nazia, fifteen, is halfway through a chemistry worksheet when Ammi's cousins arrive without warning. 'Nazia, tea and pakoras, jaldi!' Her brother Faiz, fourteen, keeps watching the cricket. Nazia fries pakoras for an hour. The worksheet stays blank.
Wednesday: In the library, Nazia tells her classmate Anirban, 'I love having guests. I just hate that it's always me.' Anirban asks, 'Have you told your Ammi that?'
Friday: More guests. This time Nazia says quietly, 'Ammi, I have a test tomorrow. Can Faiz make the tea today?' Ammi pauses, then calls, 'Faiz! Kitchen.' Faiz groans, but goes. Nazia serves the plates with a smile, then returns to her books.

qa.q: What was Nazia working on when the guests arrived on Tuesday?
qa.a: A chemistry worksheet.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when she told Anirban, 'I just hate that it's always me'?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and resentful about the unfairness, even though she still enjoys having guests.

qa.q: What made Friday go better?
qa.a: Nazia asked Ammi calmly with a clear reason, and Ammi shared the job by calling Faiz, so hosting stayed warm but fairer.

qa.q: How might Faiz see being called into the kitchen?
qa.a: Faiz may feel annoyed at first, but it shows him that serving guests is his job too, not only his sister's.

grounding: Illustrates a teenage daughter repeatedly pulled from study to serve unexpected guests while her brother is left alone, and a fairer sharing of hosting once she speaks up.

passage:
Afreen's board chemistry exam was at nine the next morning, and she and Avni were on a video call, halfway through organic reactions, when the doorbell rang. Khala, Khalu and four cousins, unannounced from Aligarh.

"Afreen, chai for everyone," Ammi called. "And the samosas from the freezer."

Afreen looked at her notes, then at her brother Saif, sprawled on the sofa with his phone. He had no exam. He didn't move.

"Why can't Saif make it?"

"Beta, he's a boy, he doesn't know how."

"Then he can learn tonight."

A small silence. Khala laughed. Ammi's cheeks went pink. Then she said, "Saif. Kitchen. Afreen will show you once, then she's going back to study."

Saif grumbled, but he poured the tea. Afreen was back on the call in eight minutes.

qa.q: When was Afreen's chemistry exam?
qa.a: Afreen's board chemistry exam was at nine the next morning.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when she asked 'Why can't Saif make it?'
qa.a: Afreen felt frustrated and treated unfairly, pulled from exam study while her brother with no exam stayed on the sofa.

qa.q: What made the outcome fairer?
qa.a: Ammi agreed that Saif would serve after one quick lesson, so the guests were still honoured while Afreen got back to her exam.

qa.q: How might Saif feel about being sent to the kitchen?
qa.a: Saif grumbled, perhaps embarrassed or put out, but he still poured the tea.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl pulled from exam study to serve surprise guests while her brother is left alone, and a fairer sharing of the serving.

passage:
Every Sunday it was the same. The bell would ring, a relative would appear at the Dadar flat, and Mummy would call, "Sarita, paani, chai!"

This Sunday Sarita was halfway through writing her debate speech for Monday. Kishore, her younger brother, was downstairs playing cricket.

She served Mama and Mami tea, then biscuits, then more tea, then washed the cups. Her speech lay on the bed, half a page long.

Mami said, "Such a good girl. Kishore is out?"

"Boys will be boys," Mummy laughed.

Sarita put the tray down harder than she meant to.

Papa noticed. After the guests left, he called down from the balcony. "Kishore! Up. Next Sunday you're on chai duty." Then, to Sarita: "Finish your speech. I'll wash these."

qa.q: What was Sarita writing when the relatives came?
qa.a: Sarita was writing her debate speech for Monday.

qa.q: What does Sarita putting the tray down hard suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt frustrated and resentful at serving all afternoon while Kishore played cricket and was excused as a boy.

qa.q: What did Papa do that made things fairer?
qa.a: He noticed, gave Kishore next Sunday's chai duty, and washed the cups himself so Sarita could finish her speech.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the afternoon?
qa.a: Mummy probably sees it as ordinary hospitality and a daughter's help, not noticing the unfairness in 'boys will be boys'.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl repeatedly pulled from study to serve relatives while her brother plays, and a parent correcting the unfairness.

passage:
"Ganga! Chai for Chachaji and Chachi!" Ma called.
Ganga looked up from her maths book. "Ma, I have a test tomorrow."
"Guests don't wait, beta."
"Lokesh has nothing tomorrow."
From the bed, Lokesh looked up from his comic. "Me? I don't know how to make chai."
"You make instant noodles every night," Ganga said.
"That's different."
"It's water and boiling. Same thing."
Ma stood in the doorway, hands on hips, looking from one to the other. "She has a point."
Lokesh groaned and rolled off the bed. "Fine. Ganga, how much sugar?"
"Two spoons for Chachaji. None for Chachi. And ask them how the drive was, don't just plonk it down."
"Yes, madam."
Ma laughed and went back to the guests. Ganga opened her book again, smiling.

qa.q: How much sugar does Chachaji take?
qa.a: Two spoons for Chachaji.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she pointed out that Lokesh has nothing tomorrow?
qa.a: Ganga felt frustrated at the unfairness of being pulled from test study while Lokesh was free.

qa.q: What made the solution work?
qa.a: Ma listened and agreed, and Lokesh took the chai duty, so the guests were still honoured and Ganga could study.

qa.q: How might Lokesh see being asked to make chai?
qa.a: Lokesh first resists, unsure of himself, but goes along with good humour once Ma backs Ganga.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl called away from study to serve guests while a sibling relaxes, and the serving being shared more fairly.

passage:
It's a few months ago now, but I still remember that Sunday. I, Ayesha, was the only daughter at home, sitting at the dining table with my chemistry book spread out, two days before the board exam. The doorbell rang. Six relatives from Aligarh, unannounced. Ammi called, "Ayesha, chai banao, jaldi." My brother Wasim was lying on the sofa playing a phone game. Nobody called him.
I made tea, then pakoras, then more tea. Two hours. My notes lay untouched. Every time I passed the sofa, Wasim was still playing. I smiled at the guests and felt boiling inside.
That night I didn't shout. I told Ammi quietly, "I love serving guests. But Wasim can boil water too. Especially in exam week." Ammi was silent a long time. Then she said, "You're right." Now when guests come, Wasim carries the tray. He spills a little. That's fine.

qa.q: What was Wasim doing while Ayesha served the guests?
qa.a: He was lying on the sofa playing a phone game.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel while serving the guests during exam week?
qa.a: She felt angry and resentful, boiling inside while smiling at the guests, because her study time was taken and her brother was left alone.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha's approach that night work?
qa.a: She spoke quietly and fairly, honouring guests while asking that her brother share the serving, which let Ammi see the unfairness.

qa.q: How might Ammi have seen the situation before Ayesha spoke?
qa.a: Ammi probably called her daughter out of habit, without noticing that Wasim was never asked or that exams were close.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager pulled from study to serve relatives while her brother is left alone, and how fairness in who serves matters.
